content_summary: Scanner premise check: the scanner said 'EXA fetched the page; abstract captured', but that abstract could not be verified here; the design (event study / DiD), sample size and estimates of the target paper are UNKNOWN, so none are recorded. Crossref/DOI/posting date/73 pp are scanner claims, unverified here. Verified facts about Lin's related work: (1) Real Estate Economics 2024, 'From Vacancy to Verdancy? The Impact of Land Options on the Timing of Vacant Lot Investment' (Lin; CSUF news story): LandCare, run by the Pennsylvania Horticultural Society, reduces time in vacancy; zoning relaxed to allow a garden shortens the time from entry to exit of vacancy status. (2) Lincoln Institute WP, April 2026 (53 pp), Lin sole author. Figures with printed-page locators (pdftotext of the PDF): p.2 'Philadelphia, as of 2010, had about 40,000 privately and publicly owned vacant lots, with 89 percent of privately owned vacant lots over 11 years delinquent in paying property taxes (Econsult 2010).' p.2 Lin's own back-of-envelope: with a 90 percent delinquency rate, a 2 percent property-tax rate and 31,000 privately owned vacant lots valued at $1.9 billion, 'the property tax revenue loss associated with privately owned vacant properties subject to tax delinquency is estimated to be $26.5 million per year', which 'well exceeds the $20 million a year in total city spending across more than ten municipal agencies maintaining vacant properties in Philadelphia (Schilling and Hodgson 2013)'. [An illustrative calculation resting on assumptions, not an estimate from the data.] Cost: upfront cleanup about $1,500 per property and annual upkeep about $300 (Lin's Cost of Stabilization section, citing a PHS field specialist); annualised $450 per year per property at a 10 percent discount rate. Table 1 (printed p.27/28): weighted ATE of greening on log sale price of nearby sales 0.0460*** (SE 0.015), unweighted 0.0205 (SE 0.025), 84,131 repeated-sales observations 2007-2019, 1,000-foot radius; text: 'a property within 1,000 feet can benefit from the amenity, with a 4.6 percent average increase of the sale price in the subsequent transaction.' Figure 6 text: effect about 12.5 percent when 8-20 lots greened within 1,000 ft, approximately zero when only 1-2 are greened; 8.9 percent for lots under 891 sq ft, 4.2 percent for 891-1,540, 3.0 percent above 1,540. Lin's paper names land banking (Philadelphia Land Bank, operational 2015) and delinquent-lot acquisition barriers as policy levers. Nothing in what was read addresses land value versus improvement assessment or assessment behaviour; the Georgist angle is indirect (greening as a cheap interim use that raises neighbouring values and preserves the redevelopment option; high delinquency means conventional property tax is weakly collected on vacant land).

(b) concepts/speculative-vacancy.md, last sentence of the 'Vacancy is the visible tip' bullet: 'outcome literature tests construction and density, not emptiness counts alone.' Possible one-line addition about greening as an interim use that shortens time in vacancy (Lin 2024, peer-reviewed, B/A-). uncertainties: Everything about the target paper's design and results is unknown. Whether the Oct 2026 paper is open elsewhere (author site, CSUF repository) is unknown; searches returned nothing. Scanner said 'complements Doucet vacant-land piece': research/doucet-does-georgism-work exists but only mentions a San Francisco vacant-lot spot check, so the complement is loose. Lin's Philadelphia delinquency figures come from Econsult 2010 via Lin and are 16 years old. Whether PHS and Dept of Revenue primaries serve openly was not established (PHS 403). The scanner's tag 'GEORGIST_STRONG' overstates relevance: the topic is delinquency resolution via greening, not land-versus-building taxation.

title: The Nordic Growth Machine: How Land Value Shapes Urban Futures (Kyronviita, Jokela and Merilainen; Tampere Urban Research Perspectives, 14 Oct 2026)
what_was_fetched: Blog post in full, ordinary request, HTTP 200 (item2-tampere-blog-landvalue.txt; raw item2-blog-raw.html). NGM2026 site (ngm2026.hi.is): home, program and sessions pages fetched openly (item2-ngm-home.txt, item2-ngm-program.txt, item2-ngm-sessions.txt, item2-ngm-special-sessions.txt): the programme lists the session '(De)Valuing land: Speculation, Housing and Residents' in room HT-104, 15:20-17:00 slot (day heading not captured), under the 'Urban Housing' theme; no abstracts, presenter names or papers are served for it. Kiviaho's University of Helsinki research-portal profile and her publication page (item2-kiviaho-portal.txt, item2-kiviaho-eps.txt). Her European Planning Studies PDF (CC BY on the portal) returned a Cloudflare 403; not retried, recorded as refusal (item2-kiviaho-eps-pdf-refusal-403.txt). No published version by Merilainen and Heldt Cassel on Kemi/Keminmaa found by search.
verdict: REJECT as a citable source (Tier 2 university research blog; summarises unpublished conference talks; no figures, no LVT content). BACKLOG lead only: Kiviaho (2026), 'Planning for shrinkage through municipal real estate management', European Planning Studies, 1 Sept 2026, DOI 10.1080/09654313.2026.2722269 (peer reviewed, CC BY on the Helsinki portal; full text not reached here), as a possible NEW research page only if a shrinking-city / municipal vacant-property angle is wanted; low Georgist yield. No ENRICH.
claim_grade: D for the blog as a source of claims (Tier 2 under 4c: institutional research blog written by session co-organisers about their own session; claims belong to the presenters; unrefereed conference talks). Kiviaho EPS article if later read: A/B, Tier 1 (peer-reviewed, academic).
content_summary: The post is narrative, with no data. Exact wording of the claims it carries: 'In large urban areas, coalitions of local governments, developers, firms, and public organizations frequently form around growth-inducing urban development projects (Logan & Molotch, 2007).' / 'As a result, land values rise, along with the value of housing assets built upon it.' / 'in urban areas where land values are comparatively low, stagnant, or declining ... growth coalitions tend to be absent. Here, land and housing assets are often subject to speculation around potential value decline.' Presenters named: Eija Merilainen and Susanna Heldt Cassel (Kemi and Keminmaa, Northern Finland; 'housing crises take multiple forms', 'limited rental options despite vacancies'); Annamari Kiviaho ('three Finnish municipalities'; 'Local governments are demolishing vacant, municipal owned rental housing to reduce oversupply, facilitating property transactions'); Matthew Howells (Danish housing associations in growth-oriented redevelopment partnerships; the post spells it Howells then Howell); Salla Jokela with Markus Laine and Aurora Luukkanen (Libeskind-designed Tampere Deck Arena; images as symbolic capital); Mikko Kyronviita (waterfront leisure assetization; 'rising land values and new forms of exclusion'). Scanner premise errors: (1) 'Kiviaho ... three municipalities': the blog says three, but a web-search snippet (a project page, not fetched or verified here) describes interviews with 15 people in four South Savo municipalities for a conference talk 'Local Responses to Housing and Real Estate Market Challenges in Shrinking Regions' (2026), so the count is inconsistent between sources; do not carry it. (2) The scanner calls it 'Lincoln Land Lines class' institutional tier: it is a department blog by the session organisers, weaker than Land Lines (editorial magazine of a Tier 1 institution). (3) The date of the session was not on the programme text captured; the blog gives only 'June 2026, right after Midsummer' (programme dates 22-25 June 2026). (4) Scanner's 'speculation/land value tax' relevance: the post never mentions taxation of land.
existing_wiki_coverage: Digest: research/tornberg-anti-growth-machine (Tornberg 2026, Antipode, inverts Logan and Molotch; 'growth machine' framing is already there and concepts/nimbyism links it); research/falkenbach-helsinki-land-lease-information-capitalization (Helsinki land leases); research/lyytikainen-finland-three-rate (Finnish three-rate property tax and construction); benefits/split-rate-increases-construction (includes Finnish case); places/denmark; places/norway; concepts/land-banking (Stockholm). No page on shrinking cities, Finnish municipal demolition, housing assetization (Aalbers) or Kemi/Keminmaa; no Logan and Molotch book page. No anchor proposed since no ENRICH.
uncertainties: Session abstracts and presenter list not openly served by ngm2026.hi.is, so the post is the only record of what was presented. Kiviaho's EPS full text blocked (403); the article's findings are unknown here. Whether Merilainen and Heldt Cassel have a published paper: not found. The blog's own reference list (Aalbers 2015, Adkins et al. 2020, Logan and Molotch 2007) is secondary theory, which could be cited directly if needed.
